subject: biology
title: Unit 1 practice exam
summary: A timed practice exam for all of Unit 1, with six short-answer questions and model answers plus 20 multiple-choice questions on cells, membranes, the cell cycle, stem cells, plant and animal systems and homeostasis.
body:
This practice exam covers the whole of Unit 1. Try it under exam conditions first, then mark it honestly using the worked solutions. The multiple-choice questions come after the written section, and each one has a full explanation.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 75 minutes in total. Allow about 25 minutes for the 20 multiple-choice questions and 50 minutes for the short-answer section.
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes or textbook. A basic calculator is allowed.
- **Marks:** the short-answer section is worth 30 marks. Count one mark for each multiple-choice question (20 marks), giving 50 marks in total.
- Do every question before looking at any solution. When you mark, give yourself a mark only when your answer contains the point listed in the solution. Then go back to the matching lesson for any topic you dropped marks on.

## Topics covered

- Cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and surface area to volume ratio
- Organelles and compartmentalisation
- The plasma membrane and transport (diffusion, osmosis, active transport, bulk transport)
- The cell cycle, mitosis, binary fission, apoptosis and cancer
- Stem cells and potency
- Plant systems: xylem, phloem, transpiration and translocation
- Animal systems: digestive, endocrine and excretory systems
- Homeostasis: the stimulus–response model, negative feedback, temperature, blood glucose and water balance
- When homeostasis fails: type 1 diabetes, hyperthyroidism and diabetes insipidus
- Scientific investigation skills

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (5 marks)

A student modelled cells as agar cubes of three sizes.

| Cube side length (cm) | Surface area (cm²) | Volume (cm³) | SA:V |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6 | 1 | ? |
| 2 | 24 | 8 | ? |
| 4 | ? | 64 | ? |

a) Complete the table by calculating the missing values. (2 marks)

b) Use your answer to explain why cells are usually very small. (2 marks)

c) Give one way a large cell can increase its surface area without changing its volume much. (1 mark)

### Question 2 (5 marks)

Strips of potato of equal mass were placed in sucrose solutions for one hour and then reweighed.

| Sucrose concentration (M) | Percentage change in mass |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | +18 |
| 0.2 | +6 |
| 0.4 | −4 |
| 0.6 | −12 |

a) Explain why the potato strip in 0.0 M sucrose gained mass. (2 marks)

b) Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic to the potato cells, and explain how you worked it out. (2 marks)

c) Describe how the cells in the 0.6 M solution would look under a microscope. (1 mark)

### Question 3 (5 marks)

a) State what happens during the S phase of the cell cycle. (1 mark)

b) A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. State the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell, and whether the daughter cells are genetically identical. (1 mark)

c) Explain how mutations in a tumour suppressor gene can lead to cancer. (2 marks)

d) State one way apoptosis is different from death by injury (necrosis). (1 mark)

### Question 4 (5 marks)

A bean plant was placed in a sealed glass box, and the rate of water uptake was measured as conditions inside the box changed.

a) The humidity inside the box rose steadily. Predict and explain the effect on the rate of water uptake. (2 marks)

b) Explain why water can move up the xylem without the plant using ATP. (2 marks)

c) State one structural difference between xylem and phloem. (1 mark)

### Question 5 (6 marks)

Kai has type 1 diabetes. Before diagnosis, his blood glucose was often well above the normal range and he passed glucose in his urine.

a) Describe what normally happens in the body when blood glucose rises after a meal. Use the stimulus–response model. (3 marks)

b) Explain why Kai's blood glucose stayed high before treatment. (2 marks)

c) Explain why type 1 diabetes cannot be treated simply by eating less sugar. (1 mark)

### Question 6 (4 marks)

A student wanted to test whether temperature affects the rate of yeast respiration. She placed yeast and sugar solution in test tubes at 20 °C, 30 °C and 40 °C and counted the CO₂ bubbles released in five minutes. She did one trial at each temperature.

a) Identify the independent and the dependent variables. (1 mark)

b) Name two variables that should be controlled. (1 mark)

c) Explain one change she should make to improve the reliability of her results. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a) SA:V for the 1 cm cube = 6 ÷ 1 = **6 : 1**. For the 2 cm cube = 24 ÷ 8 = **3 : 1**. For the 4 cm cube, SA = 6 × 4² = 6 × 16 = **96 cm²**, so SA:V = 96 ÷ 64 = **1.5 : 1**. (1 mark for 96 cm², 1 mark for all three ratios correct.)

b) As the cube gets bigger, its SA:V falls (1 mark). A cell exchanges nutrients, gases and wastes through its surface, but it uses and makes materials throughout its volume. A large cell has too little membrane for its volume, so exchange is too slow to meet its needs (1 mark).

c) Any one: fold the membrane into microvilli; become flattened or thin; become long and narrow. (1 mark)

### Question 2

a) A 0.0 M solution (pure water) is hypotonic to the potato cells, so it has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm (1 mark). Water moved into the cells by osmosis, towards the higher solute concentration, so the strip gained mass (1 mark).

b) About **0.3 M** (accept 0.3–0.35 M) (1 mark). The isotonic concentration is where the percentage change in mass is zero; the change goes from +6 at 0.2 M to −4 at 0.4 M, so it crosses zero between them, a little above 0.3 M (1 mark).

c) The cells are plasmolysed: the plasma membrane and cytoplasm have shrunk and pulled away from the cell wall. (1 mark)

### Question 3

a) DNA replication: each chromosome is copied to form two sister chromatids. (1 mark)

b) 46 chromosomes in each, and they are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell. (1 mark; both parts needed.)

c) Tumour suppressor genes normally slow down cell division or trigger apoptosis in damaged cells (1 mark). When they mutate and stop working, damaged cells keep dividing instead of being stopped or removed, so they build up into a tumour (1 mark).

d) Any one: apoptosis is controlled or programmed; the cell breaks into membrane-bound fragments that phagocytes eat; it does not cause inflammation; the cell does not burst. (1 mark)

### Question 4

a) The rate of water uptake would fall (1 mark). Higher humidity reduces the concentration gradient of water vapour between the air spaces in the leaf and the air outside, so less water evaporates through the stomata. This lowers transpiration, so less water is pulled up and taken in (1 mark).

b) Water is pulled up by transpiration: as water evaporates from the leaves, it creates tension that pulls on the water column (1 mark). Cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) keeps the column continuous, and adhesion to the xylem walls helps it rise. These are physical forces, so no ATP is needed (1 mark).

c) Any one: xylem cells are dead and phloem cells are alive; xylem walls are thickened with lignin; xylem is hollow tubes with no end walls whereas phloem sieve tubes have sieve plates and companion cells. (1 mark)

### Question 5

a) The stimulus is a rise in blood glucose. Receptor and control centre: beta cells in the pancreas detect the rise (1 mark) and release insulin into the blood (1 mark). Effectors: body cells take up more glucose and the liver converts glucose into glycogen. Response: blood glucose falls back to the set point, and insulin release stops; this is negative feedback (1 mark).

b) In type 1 diabetes, the immune system has destroyed the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made (1 mark). Without insulin, cells do not take up glucose and the liver does not store it as glycogen, so glucose stays high in the blood (1 mark).

c) The body can still make glucose from other sources (for example, the liver breaks down glycogen and makes new glucose), and without insulin, glucose cannot be moved into cells whatever the diet. Insulin itself must be replaced. (1 mark)

### Question 6

a) Independent variable: temperature. Dependent variable: number of CO₂ bubbles released in five minutes. (1 mark; both needed.)

b) Any two: mass or volume of yeast; concentration and volume of sugar solution; type of sugar; size of test tube; time counted. (1 mark)

c) Carry out replicates, for example three trials at each temperature (1 mark), and calculate the mean. This reduces the effect of random errors and shows whether results are consistent (1 mark). (Also accept: measure the gas volume with a gas syringe instead of counting bubbles, because bubbles vary in size, giving more precise and accurate measurements.)

questions.prompt: Which observation would show that a cell is prokaryotic rather than eukaryotic?

options.A: It has ribosomes
options.B: It has a cell wall
options.C: Its DNA is in a nucleoid with no surrounding membrane
options.D: It has a plasma membrane

questions.explanation: Only prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane; their DNA sits in the nucleoid. A cell wall (B) is tempting, but plant and fungal cells also have walls, so a wall does not prove a cell is prokaryotic. All cells have ribosomes and a plasma membrane.

questions.prompt: Cell A is a cube with sides of 3 µm. Cell B is a cube with sides of 6 µm. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Cell A has a SA:V of 2 : 1 and Cell B has a SA:V of 1 : 1
options.B: Both cells have the same SA:V
options.C: Cell B has double the SA:V of Cell A
options.D: Cell A has a SA:V of 6 : 1 and Cell B has a SA:V of 3 : 1

questions.explanation: For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side. Cell A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 : 1. Cell B: 6 ÷ 6 = 1 : 1. Option C reverses the relationship: the larger cell has the smaller ratio. Option D uses the values for 1 µm and 2 µm cubes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the plasma membrane is consistent with the fluid mosaic model?

options.A: The phospholipids are fixed in place and only proteins can move
options.B: Phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways within the bilayer
options.C: The hydrophobic tails face the watery fluid inside and outside the cell
options.D: The membrane is a single layer of protein coated with lipid

questions.explanation: 'Fluid' means the phospholipids and many proteins move sideways; 'mosaic' means proteins are scattered through the bilayer. Option C is a common mix-up: it is the hydrophilic heads that face the watery fluid, while the hydrophobic tails face inwards.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells take up nitrate ions from soil where nitrate is less concentrated than in the cells. Which feature would you expect these cells to have plenty of?

options.A: Chloroplasts
options.B: Lysosomes
options.C: Smooth ER
options.D: Mitochondria

questions.explanation: Moving ions against their gradient is active transport, which needs ATP, and most ATP is made in mitochondria. Chloroplasts (A) are tempting because they are plant organelles, but root cells are underground, get no light and usually lack chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: Which process moves a large particle, such as a bacterium, into a white blood cell?

options.A: Endocytosis
options.B: Exocytosis
options.C: Facilitated diffusion
options.D: Osmosis

questions.explanation: Endocytosis (here, phagocytosis) folds the membrane around the bacterium to form a vesicle that carries it in. Exocytosis (B) is the reverse, moving material out of the cell. Bacteria are far too large for channel or carrier proteins.

questions.prompt: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. Which sequence of events is correct?

options.A: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid
options.B: Salt enters the cell and the cell bursts
options.C: Water leaves by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall
options.D: Water leaves and the cell wall collapses inward with the membrane

questions.explanation: A concentrated salt solution is hypertonic, so water leaves by osmosis and the cell becomes plasmolysed. Option D is tempting, but the cell wall is rigid and keeps its shape; it is the membrane that pulls away from it.

questions.prompt: Which shows the correct order of organelles in the pathway that makes and exports a hormone that is a protein?

options.A: Golgi → ribosome → rough ER → vesicle → plasma membrane
options.B: Ribosome → rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane
options.C: Ribosome → smooth ER → lysosome → plasma membrane
options.D: Nucleus → Golgi → rough ER → plasma membrane

questions.explanation: Proteins are made on ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi for modification and packaging, then carried in vesicles to the membrane for exocytosis. Option C is tempting but uses smooth ER, which makes lipids, and lysosomes, which digest material.

questions.prompt: A cell has completed the S phase but not yet entered mitosis. Compared with a cell in G1, it has:

options.A: half as much DNA
options.B: the same amount of DNA
options.C: twice as many separate chromosomes
options.D: twice as much DNA, with each chromosome made of two sister chromatids

questions.explanation: DNA is copied in S phase, so the DNA content doubles, but the copies stay joined at the centromere as two sister chromatids. The chromosome number has not yet changed, so option C, which counts each chromatid as a separate chromosome, is wrong.

questions.prompt: A drug stops spindle fibres from forming. At which stage would dividing cells be stuck?

options.A: G1
options.B: S phase
options.C: Before chromosomes could line up at metaphase
options.D: Cytokinesis, after the nucleus has divided

questions.explanation: Spindle fibres attach to and move chromosomes, so without them chromosomes cannot line up at the metaphase plate, and the M checkpoint stops the cycle. Option D is tempting, but the nucleus cannot divide properly without spindle fibres, so cells never reach cytokinesis.

questions.prompt: How does binary fission in bacteria differ from mitosis?

options.A: Binary fission produces genetically different cells
options.B: Binary fission does not involve DNA replication
options.C: Binary fission involves a circular chromosome and no spindle fibres
options.D: Binary fission produces four daughter cells

questions.explanation: Bacteria copy their single circular chromosome and the copies separate as the cell lengthens, with no spindle. Option B is tempting because the process is simple, but the chromosome must still be copied first, or one daughter cell would have no DNA.

questions.prompt: A mutation causes a proto-oncogene to become permanently active. What is the most likely effect?

options.A: The cell divides even without signals to divide
options.B: The cell undergoes apoptosis
options.C: The cell stops dividing
options.D: The cell becomes a stem cell

questions.explanation: Proto-oncogenes normally promote division when signalled; an oncogene acts like a stuck accelerator, driving division without signals. Option B is tempting because apoptosis removes damaged cells, but the mutation itself pushes the cell to divide, not to die.

questions.prompt: Which statement about induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells is correct?

options.A: They are collected from the inner cell mass of embryos
options.B: They are totipotent and can form a placenta
options.C: They are only multipotent, like bone marrow stem cells
options.D: They are made by reprogramming a patient's own body cells, which lowers the risk of rejection

questions.explanation: iPS cells are adult body cells reprogrammed in the laboratory to be pluripotent. Because they come from the patient, they match the patient's tissue. Option A describes embryonic stem cells, the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a sieve tube element well suited to translocation?

options.A: It is dead and lignified
options.B: It has a companion cell that supplies ATP for loading sugars
options.C: It has many chloroplasts
options.D: It carries water only upwards

questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements have few organelles, so companion cells supply the ATP needed to load sugars at the source. Option A describes xylem, not phloem. Option D is also xylem; phloem can move sugars up or down depending on where the sinks are.

questions.prompt: On a hot, windy afternoon, many plants close their stomata. What is the main cost to the plant of doing this?

options.A: Water loss increases
options.B: Translocation stops completely
options.C: Less CO₂ enters the leaf, so photosynthesis slows
options.D: Roots can no longer take up minerals by active transport

questions.explanation: Stomata are a trade-off: closing them saves water but also stops CO₂ entering, which slows photosynthesis. Option A is the opposite of what happens; closing stomata reduces water loss.

questions.prompt: Which feature of the small intestine increases the rate at which nutrients are absorbed?

options.A: Villi and microvilli that greatly increase surface area
options.B: A thick muscular wall that churns food
options.C: Acid that kills bacteria
options.D: Bile stored in the gall bladder

questions.explanation: Villi and microvilli give a huge surface area for absorption. A muscular wall (B) is tempting because it is part of the gut, but it moves and mixes food (peristalsis) rather than increasing absorption surface. Acid is made in the stomach.

questions.prompt: A hormone travels in the blood to every part of the body, yet it affects only some cells. Why?

options.A: The hormone is destroyed before it reaches most cells
options.B: Only some cells have receptors for that hormone
options.C: Hormones only enter cells by active transport
options.D: Only cells near the gland receive the hormone

questions.explanation: Only target cells with matching receptors respond. Option D is tempting, but hormones are carried in the blood throughout the body; distance from the gland does not decide which cells respond.

questions.prompt: Which substance is normally filtered at the glomerulus but then completely reabsorbed in a healthy kidney?

options.A: Urea
options.B: Red blood cells
options.C: Plasma proteins
options.D: Glucose

questions.explanation: Glucose is small enough to be filtered and is then all reabsorbed in the tubule, so normally none appears in urine. Urea (A) is filtered but mostly excreted. Red blood cells and most proteins are too large to be filtered.

questions.prompt: A person walks from a warm room into freezing air. Which response is part of negative feedback to keep body temperature stable?

options.A: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels
options.B: Increased sweating
options.C: Vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
options.D: Reduced metabolic rate

questions.explanation: In the cold, vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, cutting heat loss, and shivering generates heat. Vasodilation (A) is tempting because it involves blood vessels, but it increases heat loss and is a response to overheating.

questions.prompt: In Graves' disease, antibodies bind to TSH receptors on the thyroid. Which set of results would you expect?

options.A: High thyroxine, high TSH
options.B: High thyroxine, low TSH
options.C: Low thyroxine, high TSH
options.D: Low thyroxine, low TSH

questions.explanation: The antibodies switch the thyroid on, so thyroxine rises. High thyroxine then acts by negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so TSH falls. Option A is tempting because it seems the thyroid is being 'over-stimulated by TSH', but the stimulation comes from antibodies, not TSH.

questions.prompt: A student's balance always reads 0.5 g too high. What kind of error is this, and how does it affect the results?

options.A: Random error; it reduces precision but not accuracy
options.B: Random error; it can be removed by taking more replicates
options.C: An outlier; the result should be deleted
options.D: Systematic error; it reduces accuracy, and repeating trials will not remove it

questions.explanation: An error that shifts every reading the same way is systematic. It makes results inaccurate, and because every repeat has the same error, more trials will not fix it. The balance must be recalibrated. Option B is tempting because replicates do reduce random error, but not systematic error.
